neurological_exam.gait: BILATERAL STEPPAGE GAIT. 'Stork leg' appearance — muscle wasting more prominent distally than proximally. Tandem walking markedly impaired. Inverted champagne bottle leg shape noted.
neurological_exam.special_tests: PES CAVUS bilaterally (arch height 42 mm — elevated). HAMMER TOES bilateral. Inverted champagne bottle appearance to calves (distal muscle wasting > proximal). No Babinski. No fasciculations.

patient.chief_complaint: Painful bilateral leg cramps and progressive weakness for 10 months, family history of foot deformities
patient.history_present_illness: Steven Achterberg is a 44-year-old building contractor presenting with a 10-month history of progressive bilateral leg weakness and painful cramps, predominantly in the calves. He has always been considered 'athletic but clumsy' and recalls childhood difficulty running fast and tripping over his own feet starting around age 8. He was told he had 'flat feet' as a child and wore orthotic insoles. He notes that his father and paternal uncle both had 'bad ankles' and trouble walking in their 50s, and his teenage son has started showing similar foot deformity. His current presentation is a noticeable worsening over the past year — he can no longer run at job sites and is developing difficulty climbing ladders. He has high-arched feet (pes cavus) and has always had hammer toes. He was evaluated by a podiatrist 5 years ago who attributed this to 'high arches.' He drinks 2-3 beers most nights. His HbA1c was checked last year at 5.4% (normal). He denies bowel or bladder dysfunction. He has had no recent illness. He works in construction and uses power tools. On direct questioning, he reports that his hands have always been slightly weaker than peers ('always chose power tools over manual') and that he has had difficulty unscrewing caps. He has never been told he has a nerve problem.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: AST 52 U/L (H), GGT 88 U/L (H) — consistent with alcohol use pattern.

specialized_test.impression: ABNORMAL NCS/EMG — uniformly slow demyelinating pattern. Motor conduction velocities uniformly slow across all tested nerves bilaterally (<38 m/s throughout), without focal areas of greater slowing, conduction block, or temporal dispersion. Distal motor latencies prolonged. Sensory nerve action potentials reduced or absent bilaterally. Needle EMG: large-amplitude, long-duration, polyphasic motor unit potentials consistent with chronic reinnervation. Findings indicate a diffuse symmetric demyelinating polyneuropathy with features of long-standing chronicity. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.citation: Leonardis L et al. (2012) Alcohol and CMT neuropathy: superimposed axonal damage. Muscle Nerve 46:604-609.
results.summary: Alcohol use in CMT patients causes superimposed axonal neuropathy on background hereditary demyelination; accelerates disability progression; GGT and liver enzymes often elevated; abstinence or significant reduction is recommended for all CMT patients.

output.interpretation: Published case series document superimposed axonal neuropathy from alcohol use in CMT patients, with acceleration of disability progression. Population-level evidence indicates that abstinence or significant reduction may slow progression in CMT patients with concurrent alcohol use. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A (CMT1A, PMP22 duplication) with superimposed alcoholic axonal neuropathy

differential.key_features: Demyelinating NCS pattern overlaps with CMT; distinguish by temporal dispersion / conduction block (CIDP) vs uniform slowing (CMT1A), CSF, and history.

differential.diagnosis: HNPP (hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies)
differential.key_features: PMP22 deletion; recurrent painless mononeuropathies, not symmetric demyelinating.
Contributory, but cannot account for childhood pes cavus / hammer toes / uniform demyelinating velocities.
No diabetes; axonal length-dependent pattern not demyelinating.
No IgM paraprotein; CMT1A explains the demyelinating phenotype.

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is a cortical test and is non-contributory in peripheral nerve disease.
Head/brain CT has no role in peripheral neuropathy evaluation.
Brain MRI is not indicated in typical distal symmetric polyneuropathy without CNS signs.
Advanced cerebral imaging (PET/MRA/MRV/perfusion) has no routine role in peripheral neuropathy.
Echocardiography is not indicated unless cardiac amyloid is suspected.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated unless there is syncope or symptomatic dysautonomia with arrhythmia concern.

sequence_constraints.reason: Tier the workup — basic labs first, then targeted electrodiagnostic and tissue studies.

critical_actions: Recognize childhood pes cavus + hammer toes + symmetric uniformly slow demyelinating velocities = hereditary demyelinating neuropathy
Order CMT genetic panel (PMP22 duplication is most common, 70-80% of CMT1)
Counsel about reproductive risk (autosomal dominant) and offer genetic counseling
Address contributing alcohol use (nutritional + neurotoxic) — reduces axonal progression
contraindicated_actions: Do not give IVIG as first-line treatment for what appears to be hereditary demyelinating neuropathy
Do not delay genetic testing — incorrect CIDP label leads to inappropriate immunotherapy
key_reasoning_points: Childhood pes cavus / hammer toes are pathognomonic clues for hereditary neuropathy
CMT1A shows uniformly slow conduction velocities <38 m/s WITHOUT conduction block or temporal dispersion (vs CIDP)
Alcohol contributes superimposed axonal injury; treat both

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Alcohol explains the axonal component but not the lifelong pes cavus or uniformly demyelinating velocities.
